BofA’s Hartnett (Flow Show) says “we stay risk-off until” three things happen to reverse the tightening in financial conditions. None has yet:

▪ Central bank rate hikes end. There have been 41 in the past six months, and BofA puts December hike odds at 64% for the Fed, 76% for the ECB and 68% for the BoJ.
▪ The 10-year Treasury yield falls below 4.5%. It’s at 4.84%.
▪ Oil falls below $80. WTI is at $90 and Brent at $98.

His path out was if this month’s payroll and CPI data come in weak, December’s Fed, ECB and BoJ hikes become the “last hikes,” and “risk assets start year-end rally @ Thanksgiving.”  It seems today's jobs report quashed that.

Meanwhile, he flags an “ominous ‘double-top’” in the equal-weight S&P 500, with “no one talking ‘big top.’”

tweets.text:
Preliminary November consumer sentiment from UMich unexpectedly rises to 51.0, the highest since August, from 48.0 in October.

▪️ Current conditions 51.0 (Oct. 46.7), expectations 50.9 (Oct. 48.8), both highest since August.
▪️ Gains “concentrated primarily among independents,” up almost 10 points to 52.1, highest since August 2025. Democrats and Republicans both slipped.
▪️ Biggest stockholders went the other way: their personal finances “dropped 12% this month to their lowest reading since April,” amid “growing anxiety over a possible AI bubble.”
▪️ But AI worries “were dwarfed by cost of living concerns”: 57% said high prices have eroded their living standards, the highest since May and up from 46% in February.
▪️ Sentiment still down 10% from February, unchanged from a year ago.
▪️ 1-yr inflation expectations fall four tenths to 4.3%, lowest since August but above February’s pre-war 3.4%. 5-10 year fall one tenth to 3.4%.

October payrolls +165,000 vs. 62,000 expected, above every one of the 79 forecasts in Bloomberg’s survey (the highest was 131,000) and the most since August. Revisions added another 84,000: August +186,000 (from +133,000) and September +60,000 (from +29,000). 

The 3-month average jumped to 137,000, the best since May, from 51,000 before revisions. Private payrolls +159,000 vs. 58,000 expected.

▪️ Professional & business services +70,000, the most since July 2022 (temp help +18,600)
▪️ Health care +41,600, the most since March
▪️ Transportation & warehousing +24,800 (couriers & messengers +17,000)
▪️ Manufacturing +19,000, a fifth straight gain, to the highest since December 2024
▪️ Construction −3,000, ending a seven-month run of gains; residential specialty trades fell to the lowest since October 2022
▪️ Leisure & hospitality −13,000; information −1,000, to the least since December 2020
▪️ Federal −1,000 to 2.677 million, the lowest since May 1966
▪️ Breadth: the diffusion index rose to 57.6, with September revised up to 54.2 from 49.0

Household survey also very strong: employment +463,000 (+1.44 million over three months) and the labor force +421,000. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% (4.141% unrounded, from 4.175%). Participation rose to 61.9%, the highest since February.

Wages: average hourly earnings +0.37% vs. 0.3% expected (September revised up to +0.26% from +0.13%) and 3.12% year-over-year vs. 2.9% expected.

Aggregate weekly payrolls (total private take-home pay) +0.47% month-over-month and 4.46% year-over-year, the fastest since January. 

The 2-year yield is up about 5 basis points, and the market-implied odds of a December hike to 74% (from 67%). Equities initially dropped but mostly recovered and are now a little lower from before the release with SPX +0.1%.

The soft spots: 
-People working part time for economic reasons +339,000 to 4.84 million, pushing U-6 back up to 7.9% from 7.6%.
-Median unemployment duration rose to 11.9 weeks, the longest since November 2021.

 Bloomberg Intelligence’s Ira Jersey: “There’s nothing weak in the report at all except the underemployment rate moving a bit higher.”

"On the dealer side, this created the opposite of Wednesday’s setup, as renewed demand for protective puts left market makers with additional positive delta exposure that then needed to be offset by shorting futures, adding yet another source of selling pressure to an already vulnerable market."

Wall Street’s “fear gauges” just had their biggest day in years. So what normally happens next?

The VIX jumped 69.7% to 28.17 Thursday, its biggest one-day gain since December 2024 and second-largest since the February 2018 “Volmageddon,” per Cboe. It was also its highest close since March 30.

The VVIX (the VIX of the VIX) rose 49.3% to 134.99, its biggest one-day gain since February 2007 and its biggest point gain since Volmageddon. So traders weren’t just hedging against further stock declines, they were scrambling to hedge volatility itself.

What history says (calculations from Cboe data):
▪️ VIX up 60%+ in a day (5 prior cases since 1990): S&P 500 higher a month later all 5 times
▪️ VIX up 40%+ (24 cases): higher a month later 18 times, and a year later 22 times, by an average of almost 19%
▪️ VIX up 40%+ and VVIX up 30%+ the same day (6 cases since 2007): higher a month later every time, but a year later only 4 of 6, averaging about 4%

Big caveat with the small sample sizes, and note it can be just the start of something much bigger, like February 2020, when the S&P was down 24% a month later. 

Getting more granular, spikes from a calm base like this one have had weaker three-month follow-through. And the closest match for both gauges, February 27, 2007, saw the S&P slightly lower a year later.
